title: Low‐dose aspirin for prevention of cardiovascular mortality in patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease: A real‐world nationwide cohort study

sections.abstract:
Cardiovascular mortality risk is elevated among patients with diabetes and concurrent chronic kidney disease. However, controversy surrounds the use of aspirin for primary prevention within this population. This study aims to assess the effectiveness and safety of low‐dose aspirin for primary prevention in patients with diabetes and pre‐end‐stage renal disease.

This was a retrospective population‐based cohort study using the National Health Insurance Research Database in Taiwan. The study included adults with type 2 diabetes who were enrolled in the pre‐end‐stage renal disease pay‐for‐performance program and had no atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. We used propensity score analysis to control baseline characteristics between the two groups. Clinical outcomes including cardiovascular mortality, all‐cause mortality, major bleeding, and renal disease progression were compared between patients who first received aspirin and those who did not.

Between January 2012 and December 2015, a total of 2,155 low‐dose aspirin users and 6,737 nonaspirin users were identified. Following propensity score adjustment, aspirin use exhibited a comparable risk of cardiovascular death compared with nonaspirin users (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 1.12; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.65–1.95; P = 0.681). The risk of all‐cause mortality was similar between the two groups (aHR 1.07; 95% CI 0.92–1.24; P = 0.385). Similar risks were observed in terms of major bleeding and renal disease progression.

In patients with diabetes and pre‐end‐stage renal disease who lacked atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, low‐dose aspirin did not demonstrate a reduction in mortality. These findings do not support the use of aspirin for primary prevention in this high‐risk population.
sections.introduction:
Type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease (CKD) are established risk factors for adverse cardiovascular outcomes. Both conditions are associated with a heightened cardiovascular risk due to mechanisms involving endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and oxidative stress, culminating in accelerated atherosclerosis 1 . Additionally, CKD contributes to systemic inflammation, leading to vascular calcification and myocardial remodeling 2 . Individuals with coexisting type 2 diabetes and CKD face particularly elevated risks of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Notably, existing evidence underscores that the mortality risk among diabetes patients is notably linked to concurrent kidney disease 3 .

Despite the high cardiovascular risk in patients with type 2 diabetes and CKD, the use of aspirin for primary cardiovascular prevention has been controversial. Clinical trials focusing on type 2 diabetes patients have yielded inconsistent findings regarding the efficacy of aspirin in reducing composite cardiovascular events among those without atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) 4 , 5 , 6 . The ASCEND (A Study of Cardiovascular Events in Diabetes) study showed that aspirin prevented vascular events but also significantly increased the risk of major bleeding in diabetic patients without ASCVD at study entry 7 . A meta‐analysis stratified by baseline cardiovascular risk found that there was no significant reduction in the cardiovascular mortality in low‐dose aspirin users regardless of baseline risk categories 8 . The ineffectiveness of aspirin in primary cardiovascular prevention was also observed in patients with CKD 9 , 10 . Moreover, the increased risk in major bleeding resulting from taking aspirin is concerning because patients with CKD have a higher risk of bleeding than those without 11 .

Notably, the specific benefits and risks of aspirin usage for primary prevention in the subgroup encompassing both type 2 diabetes and CKD have not been investigated in randomized controlled trials. Because of the uncertainty regarding aspirin's appropriateness for primary cardiovascular prevention in this population, we investigated the effect of low‐dose aspirin on cardiovascular death and all‐cause mortality, major bleeding, and adverse renal events in Taiwanese patients with type 2 diabetes and coexisting CKD, excluding patients with confirmed or suspected ASCVD at baseline.
sections.methods:
This was a population‐based retrospective observational cohort study. The primary data source utilized for this study was the National Health Insurance Research Database (NHIRD). The NHIRD represents an extensive nationwide repository of insurance claim‐related information encompassing demographics, diagnostic details, inpatient and ambulatory records, as well as prescription claims data for 99% of the resident population. The data period used in this study was 2000–2018. The study protocol received approval from the Joint Institutional Review Board of Taipei Medical University (TMU‐JIRB No. N202010056). Because the data source in this study was de‐identified, the Institutional Review Board waive the requirement for individual informed consent.

The study's participant cohort was constituted of individuals who received diagnoses of both type 2 diabetes and CKD within the defined index period spanning from 1 January 2012 to 31 December 2015. To be included as a patient with diabetes, a patient was required to have at least three instances of International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision, Clinical Modification ( ICD‐9‐CM ) code 250 in either outpatient or inpatient records and to have received antidiabetic medication. To ensure the precision of the CKD diagnosis, patients were mandated to be participants in the pre‐end‐stage renal disease (ESRD) pay for performance (P4P) program. This program, instituted by the National Health Insurance Administration of Taiwan, is designed to enroll individuals with CKD stages 3b, 4, and 5 who have not yet commenced dialysis. Engagement in this program is voluntary, offering pre‐ESRD care administered by a multidisciplinary team and entailing comprehensive evaluations on a tri‐monthly basis. Since patients in the pre‐ESRD P4P program were closely monitored with clear documentation of CKD staging, using this cohort can provide additional information on patient characteristics and clinical outcomes. Patients were excluded from the study if they had cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, or peripheral vascular disease. Key exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) having a diagnosis of type 1 diabetes; (2) having received anticoagulants or other antiplatelet drugs; (3) having a history of acute coronary syndrome, nonfatal ischemic stroke, transient ischemic attack, systemic embolism, heart failure, or peripheral artery disease; (4) having received percutaneous transluminal angioplasty for peripheral artery disease, coronary artery bypass graft surgery, percutaneous coronary intervention, a myocardial perfusion scan, or a treadmill exercise test before the index date; (5) and having a diagnosis of tachyarrhythmia, deep vein thrombosis, or pulmonary embolism before the index date. The use of aspirin was identified from prescription claims using Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) codes and reimbursement codes. We chose low‐dose aspirin (75–162 mg) as our study drug based on guidelines for the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease 12 . For aspirin users, the index date was defined as the date of initiating aspirin therapy. To avoid immortal time bias, each aspirin user was paired with a nonaspirin user, who was assigned the same index date. The process of patient selection is represented in Figure 1 . Recognizing the augmented risk of morbidity and mortality among patients with diabetes exhibiting target organ damage, diabetes severity was assessed using the diabetes complications severity index, a robust tool renowned for its predictive capacity regarding mortality and hospitalization within the diabetic population 13 . Patients were rated on the basis of the presence and severity of target organ damage related to diabetes. A higher score on this index was indicative of more pronounced and severe diabetic complications. The maximum score was 13. The diagnosis codes for baseline comorbidities and ATC codes for medications are provided in Table S1 . We did not include glucagon‐like peptide 1 agonists and sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors in baseline demographics because these drugs were not commonly used in clinical practice during the study period and most were not covered by National Health Insurance.

Patient selection process. Pre‐ESRD, Pre end‐stage renal disease.

The outcomes of interest in this study were effectiveness and safety outcomes. The effectiveness outcomes of this study were cardiovascular death and all‐cause mortality. Cardiovascular death was defined as death due to heart failure, sudden cardiac death, ventricular arrhythmia, ischemic heart disease, ischemic cerebrovascular disease, and peripheral arterial disease. The safety outcomes were major bleeding and renal disease progression. The criteria for major bleeding were bleeding at a critical site and bleeding requiring transfusion. Renal disease progression was defined as progression from stage 3b or 4 to stage 5 CKD or initiation of renal replacement therapy and verified using records in the pre‐ESRD P4P program. The disease diagnosis codes for the study outcomes are provided in Table S1 . Patients were censored if the outcome of interest or death occurred or switched groups. Otherwise, patients were followed up to 3 years.

For statistical analysis, the propensity score was used to reduce potential selection bias. We used standardized mortality ratio weighting (SMRW) to estimate the average treatment effect among the treated population. SMRW has the advantages of increasing precision by keeping most treated samples in the analysis and reducing the potential for estimating the treatment effect in patients with contraindications 14 , 15 . Each patient was given a weight based on propensity score considering the baseline characteristics and medications. Aspirin users were given a weight of 1, and nonaspirin users were weighted with a ratio of propensity score to 1 minus the propensity score. The comparison of baseline characteristics between aspirin users and nonaspirin users was expressed as the standardized mean difference. A value of less than 0.1 indicated a negligible difference. Survival analysis was conducted using the Kaplan–Meier method and a conditional Cox proportional hazard regression. The model was adjusted for the baseline characteristics and medications. The nonaspirin group served as the reference group for analyses. A value of P < 0.05 indicated significance. Analyses were performed using SAS/STAT 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA) and R Statistical Software (v4.1.2; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).
sections.results:
A total of 8,892 patients with type 2 diabetes and pre‐ESRD who had no ASCVD at baseline were included in the analysis. Of the total patients, 2,155 were new low‐dose aspirin users and 6,737 were nonaspirin users (Figure 1 ). Baseline demographics, comorbidities, and medications are shown in Table 1 . Low‐dose aspirin users were older, had a higher diabetes complications severity index, and had more comorbidities, such as hypertension and hyperlipidemia, compared with nonaspirin users. After SMRW, there were 2,152 nonaspirin users and 2,155 aspirin users entering the outcome analyses. The baseline characteristics became well‐balanced between the two groups after SMRW. Most patients (96%) had stage 3b or 4 CKD, and the average diabetes complications severity index was 2.6. The mean follow‐up period was 2.8 and 2.3 years in the nonaspirin users and aspirin group, respectively.

Baseline characteristics before and after SMRW

Diabetes complications severity index contains seven categories of complications (cardiovascular disease, nephropathy, retinopathy, peripheral vascular disease, stroke, neuropathy, and acute metabolic complications), each of which was rated (no abnormality = 0, some abnormality = 1, severe abnormality = 2), with a total maximum score of 13; Charlson/Deyo index = myocardial infarction, congestive heart failure, peripheral vascular disease, cerebrovascular disease, dementia, chronic pulmonary disease, rheumatologic disease, peptic ulcer disease, mild liver disease, diabetes, diabetes with chronic complications, hemiplegia or paraplegia, renal disease, moderate or severe liver disease, acquired immune deficiency syndrome.

CKD, chronic kidney disease; SMD, standardized mean difference; SMRW, standardized mortality ratio weighting.

The incidence of effectiveness outcomes and Kaplan–Meier curves are shown in Table 2 and Figure 2 , respectively. The incidence of cardiovascular death was 4.74 vs 4.34 per 1,000 patient‐years in low‐dose aspirin users and nonaspirin users, respectively. The risk of cardiovascular death was similar between the two groups, with an adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) of 1.12 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.65–1.95; P = 0.681). All‐cause mortality rates were high but similar between the two groups (aHR: 1.07; 95% CI: 0.92–1.24; P = 0.385). Subgroup analysis was performed based on age, gender, comorbidities, and the diabetes complications severity index. No differences were found between the aspirin and nonaspirin groups in terms of cardiovascular death and all‐cause mortality in any of the subgroups. The results of the subgroup analysis are presented in Figures S1 and S2 .

Incidence (per 1,000 patient‐years) and adjusted hazard ratio of effectiveness and safety outcomes

aHR, adjusted hazard ratio.

Effectiveness outcomes: low‐dose aspirin vs nonaspirin. Low‐dose aspirin group was associated with similar risks of cardiovascular death (a) and all‐cause mortality (b) compared with the nonaspirin group.

The incidence of safety outcomes and Kaplan–Meier curves are shown in Table 2 and Figure 3 , respectively. The incidence of major bleeding was high in the study population (26.96 and 31.53 per 1,000 patient‐years for low‐dose aspirin users and nonaspirin users, respectively) without a significant difference between the two groups (aHR: 0.85; 95% CI: 0.69–1.04; P = 0.116). In addition, the risk of renal disease progression was not significantly different between the two groups despite the high incidence of renal events in this study cohort (75.97 and 84.68 per 1,000 patient‐years for low‐dose aspirin users and nonaspirin users, respectively; P = 0.073).

Safety outcomes: low‐dose aspirin vs nonaspirin. Low‐dose aspirin users had similar risks of major bleeding (a) and renal disease progression (b) to nonaspirin users.
sections.discussion:
This study found that the use of low‐dose aspirin in Taiwanese patients with type 2 diabetes and pre‐ESRD who had no ASCVD at baseline did not protect against mortality. This is the largest study to investigate the effect of low‐dose aspirin in this high cardiovascular risk population. A prospective cohort study evaluated the effect of aspirin (100 mg/day) on primary prevention in 564 patients with diabetic nephropathy. The study found that aspirin neither reduced the risk of cardiovascular death nor increased the risk of major bleeding after 8 years of follow‐up 16 . Another post‐hoc subgroup analysis from a randomized controlled trial, which enrolled 2,539 patients with type 2 diabetes and without ASCVD in Japan, had similar findings 17 . This post‐hoc analysis investigated the efficacy of 81–100 mg/day of aspirin on primary atherosclerosis prevention in patients with type 2 diabetes and coexisting renal dysfunction. In patients with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of <60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , low‐dose aspirin did not reduce the risk of atherosclerotic events, although some benefit was seen in patients with eGFRs of 60–89 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . On the contrary, a randomized controlled trial, which was originally designed to examine the efficacy and safety of polypill and aspirin in subjects without cardiovascular disease who were at intermediate cardiovascular risk, performed a subgroup analysis to examine the efficacy of aspirin among patients with different levels of eGFR 18 , 19 . While aspirin did not reduce major adverse cardiovascular events compared with placebo in subjects with a baseline eGFR ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events was lower among aspirin users in subjects with baseline eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 18 . However, the interaction of eGFR and the treatment effect was not statistically significant. The paucity of compelling evidence has precluded international guidelines from endorsing aspirin use for primary prevention 12 , 20 , 21 . In patients with diabetes with high cardiovascular risk, low‐dose aspirin may be considered for primary prevention if no contraindication exists, per the recommendations of the European Society of Cardiology and the American Diabetes Association 12 , 20 . Although patients with type 2 diabetes and coexisting CKD have considerable cardiovascular risk, the results of this study and the relevant studies do not support the use of low‐dose aspirin to prevent atherosclerotic cardiovascular events.

The lack of benefit of aspirin in patients with diabetes and CKD may be explained by high residual platelet activity and the hypercoagulable state associated with both diabetes and CKD 22 , 23 , 24 . Patients with CKD had higher platelet activity at baseline and an attenuated response to aspirin compared with patients without CKD 24 . In addition to traditional risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, and smoking, the development of ASCVD may result from other mechanisms that are more prominent in patients with CKD 2 . Accelerated vascular calcification resulting from altered smooth muscle cell differentiation leads to arterial stiffness and left ventricular hypertrophy 25 , 26 . Inflammatory cytokines and the production of reactive oxygen species in response to kidney injury result in systemic inflammation that also contributes to changes in vasculature 2 , 27 . These pathological mechanisms are not influenced by antiplatelet drugs, which may explain the lack of a protective effect of aspirin against ASCVD in this study population. Moreover, although patients with diabetes treated with low‐dose aspirin exhibit aspirin resistance, higher doses can partially overcome the resistance 28 . Higher doses of aspirin may be necessary to prevent ASCVD in this study population.

The present study found that low‐dose aspirin had no effect on CKD progression. This finding is consistent with other studies 13 , 16 , 29 , 30 , 31 . A randomized trial enrolled CKD patients, which included non‐dialysis, dialysis, and renal transplant patients, showed that low‐dose aspirin neither affect serum creatinine nor increase the risk of initiation of dialysis compared with placebo 30 . Another large‐scale prospective cohort study in CKD patient also showed no difference in renal disease progression and initiation of renal replacement therapy between aspirin and nonaspirin users 29 . Although there are study groups that proposed a potential renoprotective effect of aspirin 10 , 32 , high quality evidence is scarce and our result does not support this hypothesis.

This study has limitations. Due to the study's design, residual bias might exist, including confounding by indication and unmeasured confounders. To reduce confounding by indication, our exclusion criteria were extensive. We used ICD‐9‐CM codes to identify patients with ASCVD, and we used procedure codes to exclude patients who had received revascularization. We also excluded patients who were suspected of having ASCVD identified by a myocardial perfusion scan and a treadmill exercise test. Use of the propensity score and SMRW should have resulted in minimal residual bias in this study. However, some variables that may influence cardiovascular risk, such as smoking habit, obesity, hemoglobin A1c level, blood cholesterol, and blood pressure are not available in the National Health Insurance Research Database. Despite this limitation, we took into account commonly used medications for these conditions when conducting the analyses, including antihypertensive drugs, lipid‐lowering drugs, and antidiabetic drugs. Additionally, patients were censored if aspirin was discontinued, limiting the follow‐up period. However, given that the patients in the present study were in the later stages of CKD (stage 3b‐5) with a high mortality rate, the impact of the limited follow‐up period may be relatively small. A large‐scale randomized controlled study is necessary to confirm the role of low‐dose aspirin in patients with both diabetes and CKD.

In conclusion, the use of low‐dose aspirin in patients with type 2 diabetes and coexisting stage 3b–5 CKD neither reduce the risk of cardiovascular death and all‐cause mortality, nor increase the risk of major bleeding and renal disease progression. Our results do not support prescribing low‐dose aspirin routinely for primary prevention in patients with diabetes and pre‐ESRD.
